analysis.one_liner: Lets farmers and independent shops legally repair modern farm equipment locked by manufacturer software.
analysis.headline: The bill sits in the House Judiciary Committee with no cosponsors and no action since its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: Modern tractors, combines, and other farm machines are run by embedded computers, and manufacturers use software locks and copyright law to restrict who can diagnose and fix them. The bill would change federal copyright law so farmers and independent repair shops can bypass those locks to diagnose, maintain, and repair farm equipment, and so shops can make and sell the tools needed to do it. It was introduced in March 2026 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmers and ranchers, who could fix their own machines or use independent repair shops instead of paying dealer rates or waiting days for an authorized technician during planting and harvest. Independent repair shops and aftermarket parts makers gain a legal market in repair tools and services.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends federal copyright law (Section 1201, the anti-circumvention provision that makes bypassing digital locks illegal) so that bypassing a software lock for the purpose of diagnosing, maintaining, or repairing farm equipment is not a violation [S2].

It also protects people who make, import, or sell tools and parts for repairing farm equipment, so independent shops and suppliers can offer the bypass tools and diagnostics that manufacturers currently restrict [S2].
It covers any farm equipment that depends on attached or embedded digital electronics to function — effectively all modern tractors, combines, and similar machines [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Farm equipment manufacturers and their dealers, who currently control diagnosis and repair through software locks, proprietary tools, and authorized-service channels, and who would lose some repair revenue and control over their machines after sale.

drawbacks.text: The exemption is written broadly: it shields anyone who bypasses software locks on farm equipment for 'repair' purposes and anyone trafficking in bypass tools for that equipment, which manufacturers and safety regulators have historically argued could enable unsafe modifications or tampering with engine, emissions, and safety software under the label of repair [S2].

The bill is narrower than many right-to-repair proposals — it covers only agricultural equipment, so the same software-lock problem would remain for cars, phones, medical devices, and other consumer products [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For farmers the benefit is concrete: faster, cheaper repairs on machines that can cost hundreds of dollars per hour of downtime during a short harvest window. The cost falls on manufacturers, whose software-lock restrictions are widely criticized as a way to charge for service that owners could perform themselves. The main honest concern is the breadth of the exemption, which could shield some modifications that go beyond genuine repair; a tighter definition of permissible repair would address that without giving up the core benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has sat without cosponsors, a hearing, or a vote since March 2026.

narrative.text: Rep. Victoria Spartz introduced the Farm Freedom to Repair Act on March 5, 2026 [S1].
The House referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day, and no further action appears in the bill's history [S4].
No other House member has cosponsored the bill [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has not advanced, farm equipment makers keep the status quo: their software locks remain fully enforceable and dealer service networks keep the repair business.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Equipment makers keep the repair monopoly for now

for.name: Rep. Victoria Spartz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and championed the right of farmers to repair their own equipment; so far, no colleagues have joined her.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Holds the bill by referral; has taken no action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote scheduled since March 2026.

against.name: Farm equipment manufacturers
against.role: Industry whose service and parts revenue the bill would reduce
against.what_they_did: Have long argued that software locks protect safety, emissions compliance, and intellectual property, and have resisted right-to-repair legislation; no manufacturer position on this specific bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan pattern has emerged.

industries.industry: Farm equipment manufacturers (e.g. makers of computerized tractors and combines)
industries.note: These manufacturers use embedded-software locks, proprietary diagnostic tools, and authorized-dealer networks to control who can fix their machines and at what price; the bill would strip their copyright-based power to block independent repair. Their interest here runs against farmers', who pay the resulting repair costs and downtime.

industries.industry: Independent farm-equipment repair shops and aftermarket parts suppliers
industries.note: The bill makes it legal to build and sell repair and diagnostic tools for farm equipment, opening a market these shops are currently barred from serving.

Farmers gain cheaper, faster repairs and the right to work on their own machines; they bear no direct cost under the bill, though lax safety exceptions could expose them to tampering disputes with manufacturers.

analysis.trajectory: With no cosponsors and no movement in Judiciary two-plus months after introduction, the bill is unlikely to advance this Congress. Right-to-repair proposals routinely die in committee unless leadership prioritizes them; broader support, a hearing, or attachment to a larger bill would change the odds.
